claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can be fabricated by selective laser melting.
SLM-processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi exhibits a high dislocation density.
SLM-processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has a fine cellular microstructure.
SLM-processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi contains abundant nanoscale Mn2O3 precipitates at cellular boundaries.
The unusually high hardness and strength of SLM equiatomic HEAs are primarily governed by nanoscale oxide precipitates formed at cellular boundaries.
Rapid solidification promotes the formation of nanoscale Mn2O3 precipitates at cellular boundaries.
Thermal contraction during SLM generates a high dislocation density.
Fine oxide particles obstruct dislocation glide through the Orowan mechanism.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates and pre-existing high dislocation density jointly increase yield strength and hardness.
Annealing in a reducing atmosphere will lower oxygen content and reduce the number of oxide precipitates or alter their fineness.
The reducing anneal can alter oxide precipitation while minimally changing grain structure.
Post-annealing lowers the dislocation density relative to the as-built state.
As-built SLM CoCrFeMnNi is stronger than an annealed comparator at room temperature.
The SLM-built alloy retains superior mechanical properties through 700 °C.
Oxygen-rich, oxide-bearing as-built specimens will have significantly greater yield strength and hardness than reducing-annealed, oxygen-depleted specimens.
Precipitate and dislocation strengthening dominate mechanical behavior between 25 and 700 °C.
The proposed governing behavior applies to compositionally similar SLM HEAs under rapid-solidification conditions that generate dislocations and oxide precipitation.
At temperatures above 700 °C or in different alloy systems, additional strengthening or deformation mechanisms may become important.
Failure of strength and hardness to correlate significantly with fine oxide retention would falsify the proposed oxide-control hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as differing only in oxygen/oxide state, but the anneal is also expected to lower dislocation density and may alter precipitate size and grain-boundary contributions. Thus the experiment does not independently isolate oxide strengthening from dislocation or annealing effects.

The intervention says annealing may reduce precipitate 'fineness,' whereas the detailed design says it will coarsen or dissolve precipitates. Reduced fineness is ambiguous and can imply finer particles, while coarsening explicitly implies larger particles.
